abstract: Abstract Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype of breast cancer lacking targeted therapies. Although aberrant N-glycosylation is a hallmark of malignancy, the specific roles of core-fucosylated (CF) and outer arm–fucosylated (OAF) N-glycans in TNBC progression and patient survival remain underexplored. This study utilized multiplexed glycomics by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization imaging mass spectrometry to spatially profile 348 N-glycans in 59 TNBC tumors with clinical characteristics including survival data. Spatial analysis revealed distinct localization patterns of CF and OAF isomers within tumor microenvironments. Strikingly, OAF glycans, but not CF, were strongly associated with tumor stage, with expression increasing from stage I to III and then declining in stage IV. Furthermore, 68 N-glycans were significantly associated with survival outcomes; 36 (52%) of these were OAF-modified, including polylactosamine structures previously linked to metastasis in breast cancer. High expression of OAF polylactosamines correlated with poor prognosis and was detectable in early-stage TNBC tumors, underscoring their potential as prognostic biomarkers. Implications: These findings demonstrate that OAF N-glycans are dynamic, structure-specific markers of TNBC progression and survival, and their early detection and strong prognostic value highlight potential utility in patient stratification and personalized therapy.

Materials and Methods
Materials
Ethanol, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)–grade acetonitrile, methanol, water, and xylene were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific. Citraconic anhydride and 10,000 MWCO Slide-A-Lyzer dialysis units were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific). Recombinant peptide N-glycosidase F (PNGase F PRIME) and endoglycosidase F3 (Endo F3 PRIME) were obtained from N-Zyme Scientifics. α-Cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid (CHCA) and trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. H&E staining solutions were purchased from Cancer Diagnostics.
Human tissues
Deidentified TNBC tissue sections were obtained from Washington University in St. Louis tissue bank through collaboration with Dr. Graham Colditz (IRB: 201102394). Tissue analysis for the project was approved by the Institutional Review Board at The Medical University of South Carolina (Pro00099334).
Tissue preparation
Tissue preparation: CF N-glycans
Tissue slides were heated at 60°C, dewaxed with xylenes and ethanol, and rehydrated with water. Antigen retrieval was then performed using citraconic anhydride buffer (25 μL citraconic anhydride, 2 μL 12 mol/L HCl, and 50 mL HPLC-grade water, pH 3.0). Analysis of CF N-glycans was performed with Endo F3 PRIME, an enzyme for the targeted cleavage of N-glycans with a core α-1,6 fucose configuration at the GlcNAc attached to an asparagine residue. Stock 100 μg aliquots of Endo F3 PRIME were dialyzed using 10 mmol/L ammonium bicarbonate with 1 mmol/L calcium chloride buffer (pH 7.4) for 4 hours with fresh buffer added after the first 2 hours of dialysis. The enzyme was sprayed in a solution of HPLC-grade water and 35 mmol/L acetic acid (final Endo F3 buffer, pH 4) using an HTX M5 sprayer (HTX Technologies LLC). The spraying parameters included 15 passes at 25 μL/minute, 1,200 mm/minute velocity, 45°C, with a crisscross pattern, and with 10 psi nitrogen gas. Tissues were incubated at 37°C for 2 hours in humidity chambers. Matrix CHCA at a concentration of 7 mg/mL was dissolved in 50% acetonitrile/0.1% TFA and sprayed on all tissues using an HTX M5 sprayer with 10 passes at 70 μL/minute, 1,300 mm/minute velocity, 79°C, with a crisscross pattern, and with 10 psi nitrogen gas (
19
). Slides were imaged via MALDI MSI as described.
Tissue preparation: N-Glycans
After MALDI MSI analysis of CF N-glycans, washes were performed to remove released N-glycans, Endo F3 enzyme, and CHCA matrix from all tissues using ethanol, water, citraconic anhydride buffer (pH 3), and Tris buffer (pH 9; ref.
20
). After drying, PNGase F PRIME was sprayed onto slides at a concentration of 0.1 μg/μL using the HTX M5 sprayer (HTX Technologies LLC) to release remaining N-glycans, cleaving at the GlcNAc attached to an asparagine residue. Enzyme was sprayed under the following parameters: 15 passes at 25 μL/minute, 1,200 mm/minute velocity, 45°C, with a crisscross pattern, and with 10 psi nitrogen gas. Slides were then incubated for 2 hours at 37°C in a humidity chamber. CHCA matrix (7 mg/mL in 50% acetonitrile/0.1% TFA) was then sprayed onto all tissues for 14 passes at 70 μL/minute, 1,300 mm/minute velocity, 79°C, and with 10 psi nitrogen gas. Tissues were then imaged via MALDI MSI as described.
MALDI MSI analysis
A dual-source 7 T MALDI Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometer (ScimaX) was used to detect N-glycans. N-Glycans released by Endo F3 or PNGase F were collected with an identical instrument method. N-Glycans were measured in positive ion mode with a 0.8913 seconds transient time over a mass range of 730 to 4,800 m/. Acquisition was performed using a SmartBeam 2 laser size set to minimum and operating at 2,000 Hz. Laser stepping varied based on tissue size; 100 laser shots were used at each sampling point.
Data analysis and processing
H&E-stained serial tissue sections were pathologist-annotated for histopathologic comparisons. Data collected from MSI analysis were loaded into SCiLS Lab (2024b Pro, Bruker) and normalized to total ion count. Spectra were then visualized, and maximum peak intensity data were exported from visualization software. N-Glycans were identified by accurate mass and categorized based on hexose content. Proposed structures were constructed in GlycoWorkbench and based on previously published human databases (
17
,
19
–
23
). Exported peak intensities were transformed using natural log. Statistical analyses, Mann–Whitney
P
values in pairwise comparisons, ROC curves, Kaplan–Meier survival curves (Mantel–Cox test; ref.
24
), and log-rank HR calculations were performed using Prism (GraphPad 10.0.1). Additional Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated in
R
(4.4.2).
P
values <0.05 were considered statistically significant.

body:
Introduction
Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a specific subtype of breast cancer that is characterized by the absence of three key breast cancer markers: estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2. The absence of these receptors means that TNBC does not respond to common breast cancer therapies, including hormonal treatments used to treat estrogen receptor–positive breast cancers and HER2-targeted therapies used to treat HER2+ breast cancers. TNBC accounts for 15% to 20% of all breast cancer cases and is frequently diagnosed in younger women, women with
BRCA1
mutations, and women of African and Hispanic descent (
1
).
TNBC is known for its aggressive nature that results in increased rates of tumor recurrence, metastasis, and shorter overall survival compared with other breast cancer subtypes. Because of the lack of targeted therapies, chemotherapy is often the primary treatment despite its variation in efficacy (
2
). Additionally, TNBC has a greater tendency to metastasize to distant sites including the lungs and the brain, which contributes to its challenging prognosis (
3
). The aggressive nature of TNBC and the absence of targeted treatments highlight the urgent need for a better understanding of the underlying biology of the disease that can be used to develop more effective, tailored therapies for this subtype.
N-glycosylation is a posttranslational modification characterized by the enzymatic addition of carbohydrates during glycoprotein folding. The further trimming and additions of sugars to the N-linked carbohydrate is a process that is highly regulated and is essential for numerous cellular functions, including cell–cell recognition, cell adhesion, protein stability, trafficking, and signaling. N-Glycans are abundant on extracellular glycoproteins and are highly expressed on the outer layer of the cell and thus serve as molecular markers that define cell identity and facilitate cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions. They also affect signaling pathways both on the cell surface and internally, affecting various cellular responses, including those related to cancer biology (
4
,
5
). Furthermore, aberrant N-glycosylation is a well-established hallmark of cancer because of its impact on tumor growth, invasion, metastasis, immune evasion, and therapeutic responses (
6
–
8
). Significant alterations in glycosylation currently play roles in the diagnosis and prognosis of several cancers, including core fucosylation (CF) of AFP-L3 in hepatic cancer, increases in core fucose glycans in total serum profiles in pancreatic cancers, and decreased galactosylation of IgG in colorectal cancers (
6
,
9
–
13
). Identifying specific N-glycosylation alterations linked to cancer can offer valuable insights into potential diagnostic markers, prognostic indicators, and therapeutic targets.
Fucosylation is a specific type of N-glycosylation characterized by the addition of a fucose residue to an N-glycan structure. It can occur as CF, resulting from the addition of the fucose to the asparagine-linked N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc), or outer-arm fucosylation (OAF), resulting from the addition of a fucose to the outer arm of a branched N-glycan structure. Elevated CF has been connected to inflammation, heightened cancer aggressiveness, poor outcomes, increased proliferation, greater metastatic potential, and resistance to treatment (
14
). Preclinical studies have investigated the molecular processes governing CF in breast cancer and its association with poor prognosis at various stages of the disease. Serum-based studies further support this, showing elevated OAF in patients with breast cancer compared with healthy individuals (
15
). Specific N-glycan structures have been mapped to pathologist-annotated tumor, stroma, and necrotic regions within TNBC utilizing matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization (MALDI) mass spectrometry imaging (MSI; refs.
16
,
17
). In a previous study, a series of polylactosamine glycans was detected in clinically advanced HER2+ and TNBC primary breast tumors and their associated metastasis, indicating a link between those glycan structures and tumor metastasis (
17
). Glycomic profiling of N-glycans in TNBC cell lines has revealed that OAF levels increase when epithelial cells adopt a more aggressive phenotype (
18
). Notably, this study also showed that OAF decreases with mammographic density, implying an N-glycosylation switch suggestive of an OAF to CF that is involved in transitions to breast cancer. Complementary spatial glycomic analyses of normal breasts from healthy women have reported that OAF is a dominant feature of the stroma, whereas CF was more prominent in adipose tissue (
19
). To date, there are limited investigations on CF versus OAF in the TNBC microenvironment and their contribution to survival outcomes.
The present study aims to further these findings by examining changes in N-glycosylation of clinically annotated TNBC tissues with patient tumor stage, clinical outcomes, and patient survival status. N-linked CF and OAF associated with survival status in the TNBC microenvironment are investigated through multiplexed spatial glycomics imaging paired with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. This study underscores that fucose-carrying N-glycans are a critical component of the TNBC microenvironment associated with staging and survival status.

Results
Study overview
The primary aim of this study was to determine the role of alterations in fucose N-glycosylation in TNBC survival. The study used a cohort of tissues from 59 African American women with TNBC with more than 75 clinical characteristics, including age, tumor stage, tumor size, tumor grade, and survival status (
Table 1
; Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Table S1). Fucose-containing spatial regulation across TNBC tumors was investigated by multiplexed glycomics targeting either CF or OAF. The multiplexed N-glycomics approach utilized Endo F3, cleaving after the CF on the primary asparagine-linked GlcNAc, followed by PNGase F, cleaving between the protein asparagine and primary GlcNAc to release OAF as well as all other N-glycans (
Fig. 1A
). When examining data from Endo F3 analysis, 123 CF N-glycans were identified in the cohort (Supplementary Table S2). From the PNGase F analysis of all remaining glycans on the tissue, 225 N-glycans were identified (Supplementary Table S3), resulting in a total of 348 N-glycans detected across both analyses (
Fig. 1B
and
C
). An in-depth characterization of the TNBC N-glycome was established, categorizing the detected glycans by branching and the presence of fucose, sialic acid, and GlcNAc motifs (
Fig. 1D
). This analysis showed that the majority of the N-glycans detected in the TNBC microenvironment were fucosylated. Within the fucosylated N-glycans, 55% were OAF and 45% were CF. Additionally, polylactosamines represented the largest portion in both CF and OAF, yet OAF contained a higher percentage of polylactosamines (
Fig. 1E
). When examining the spatial distribution patterns, fucosylated N-glycans were heterogeneously distributed throughout TNBC tumors. However, many spatial distribution patterns reported complementary localization between the CF and OAF isomers within a tumor region that could not be otherwise differentiated by standard pathology methods (
Fig. 1F
and
G
).
Table 1.
Clinical characteristics of the study cohort. Tissue samples were obtained from African American women diagnosed and treated for TNBC at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri, between 1977 and 2016. Tumor stage was classified according to tumor, node, and metastasis criteria. Survival time was calculated as the number of months between the date of diagnosis and either the date of death or the last confirmed date the patient was known to be alive.

Heterogeneous spatial localization of CF and OAF glycan isomers within the TNBC microenvironment
The spatial localization of CF and OAF N-glycan isomers was investigated within TNBC tissues, revealing distinct and varied patterns of distribution. Localization to tumor and nontumor regions was not specific to CF or OAF but instead varied for each glycan structure (
Fig. 2
). Image segmentation was used to assign pixels from either CF or OAF expression based on intensity and localization. These data showed that both CF and OAF have distinctive contributions to the TNBC tumor microenvironment aligning with pathologic annotation (
Fig. 2A
; Supplementary Fig. S2). In certain tumors, CF and OAF seemed to have complementary expression patterns in tumor and nontumor expression (example,
Fig. 2B
). In other tumors, CF and OAF both frequently localized to the tumor microenvironment but showed distinctive expression levels altering within tumor and adjacent regions (
Fig. 2C
). The TNBC tumor microenvironment also showed gradient patterns within the tumor that seemed to be influenced by cellular content, necrosis, or stroma composition (
Fig. 2D
). Therefore, both CF and OAF showed a heterogeneous distribution throughout the tumor microenvironment, occurring in both tumor and nontumor regions with specific pathologies. Spatial localization is not dependent on the status of CF or OAF linkage and instead varies for individual N-glycan.

TNBC stages differentiate by OAF
When examining changes in N-glycosylation across the four stages of TNBC, 60 of 348 (17%) N-glycans were found to be statistically significant (ANOVA FDR-controlled
P
value < 0.05). Interestingly, none of these N-glycans were CF. Of the 60 statistically significant glycans, 45 were OAF and 15 were not fucosylated (Supplementary Table S4).
Fig. 3
shows representative images of stage I, II, III, and IV TNBC tissues for three OAF glycans with significant changes in expression across stages relative to their CF counterparts. Pathologic stains demonstrate tumor areas (
Fig. 3A
). For the OAF N-glycans that were significantly altered by stage, median intensity increased as stage increased from stage I to III. However, stage IV tumors showed a deflection and had decreasing intensxities relative to stage III (
Fig. 3B
). This change in intensity by tumor stage was not seen in CF; instead, expression remained similar throughout staging (
Fig. 3C
). Although OAF expression overall seemed to increase per staging, expression levels of all OAF glycans seemed consistent per patient sample (
Fig. 3D
). When evaluated by principal component analysis, strong clustering by stage was observed (
Fig. 3E
). In summary, TNBC stages were differentiated by distinct OAF N-glycans, showing progressive increases as stage advanced with consistent expression of all OAF N-glycans within each tumor. This suggests that OAF N-glycans, compared with CF N-glycans, may play a role throughout tumor growth progression.

Distinct fucosylated N-glycans, but not their counterpart isomers, define TNBC survival probabilities
This study identified 68 glycans that were statistically significant for patient survival (Kaplan–Meier log-rank
P
value < 0.05). Of these 68 glycans, 8 were CF, 36 were OAF, and 24 were non-fucosylated (Supplementary Table S5). Interestingly, for CF glycans (CF 2142) and (CF 2528), which were statistically significant for survival, the OAF isomer was not (
Fig. 4A
and
B
). This also held true when examining the CF isomers of statistically significant OAF glycans (OAF 1996, OAF 2158, OAF 2174, OAF 2539, and OAF 2832;
Fig. 4C–G
). This indicates that distinct fucosylated N-glycans play a significant role in patient survival compared with their isomeric counterparts, thus highlighting the importance of fucose addition to N-glycans in influencing patient prognosis. Notably, it was the higher expression of these specific fucosylated glycan structures that was associated with poor survival probability, suggesting a potential for early detectability of these prognostic markers. Indeed, several glycans associated with survival were detectable at earlier stages and could distinguish between vital status [area under the ROC curve (AUROC) >0.7;
P
value < 0.05;
Fig. 5
; Supplementary Fig. S3].

High expression levels of OAF polylactosamine N-glycans are linked to poor patient outcomes
Previously, polylactosamine N-glycans were reported as a marker for poor prognosis in TNBC and HER2+ breast cancers (
17
). The distinct structure of polylactosamine N-glycans, characterized by repeating lactosamine units (GlcNAc–galactose disaccharide), may influence cell–cell interactions and tumor behavior. In this study, 85 polylactosamine glycans were identified within the TNBC microenvironment. These included 10 OAF, 2 CF, and 1 polylactosamine glycans that were non-fucosylated. Survival analysis showed that patients with higher expression of each polylactosamine linked to poor survival (
Fig. 6
; Supplementary Table S5). Interestingly, from the first emergence of the OAF polylactosamine structure to the most extended form detected, these polylactosamines were connected to decreased survival (
Fig. 6A–D
). Additional evaluation reported that certain polylactosamines could distinguish between vital status (AUROC >0.7,
P
value < 0.009;
Fig. 6E–G
). Further assessment of image patterns showed strong detection of distinguishing polylactosamines at early stages (
Fig. 6H–J
). This supports that polylactosamines related to poor survival are detected in early stages of tumor and thus may play a role in aggressive TNBC tumors.

Discussion
This investigation demonstrates that N-glycosylation is a critical, spatially regulated component of the TNBC tumor microenvironment, with significant implications for disease progression and clinical outcomes. Previous studies have highlighted the role of CF of N-linked glycans on specific proteins, such as TGFβ, in increasing breast cancer invasiveness (
25
). Fucose-containing N-glycans have been shown to induce anti-inflammatory cytokines and differentiate T-cell phenotypes that are immunosuppressive across multiple cancer types (
26
). Likewise, aberrant CF on CD276 (B7H3) has been shown to promote immunosuppressive activity in TNBC, and its inhibition improves therapeutic response (
27
). Although these studies emphasize CF at the protein level, the current findings indicate that on a global scale, OAF exerts a more pronounced influence on tumor behavior and outcome. Here, changes in overall N-glycosylation demonstrate that OAF and CF N-glycans show some complementary but heterogeneous expression in the TNBC tumor microenvironment. OAF, but not CF, N-glycosylation was found to contribute to TNBC staging, supporting a role in tumor progression. Strong associations of OAF N-glycans with survival probabilities further implicated that distinct N-glycans contribute to TNBC tumor aggressiveness. Additionally, this study further supports that OAF polylactosamines contribute to more aggressive TNBC.
This study is the first to spatially map the distribution of CF and OAF N-glycans in a clinically annotated TNBC cohort, establishing their relevance not only in tumor biology but also in patient survival outcomes. The divergent survival associations observed between CF and OAF isomers of the same glycan likely reflect functional differences driven by the position of fucose on the glycan structure. Fucose positioning can determine whether the glycan’s role is structural, signal-modulatory, or immunologically active, with each fucose position triggering different lectins or receptors and shaping the immune landscape accordingly. Previous studies have shown that CF modifies N-glycan conformation and stability to immunoregulatory proteins, thereby indirectly tuning receptor–ligand interactions and immune checkpoint function (
28
). In contrast, terminal fucosylation or OAF forms ligands for lectins such as DC-SIGN and selectins, creating an immunosuppressive microenvironment characterized by M2 macrophages and regulatory T-cell induction (
26
,
29
). These functional consequences of fucose positioning explain why structurally similar glycans may have opposing prognostic implications.
Changes in spatial distribution suggest that specific N-glycan structures—rather than simply the presence or core fucosylation or OAF modifications—are associated with different cellular interactions or tumor subregions to influence tumor progression or outcomes. Localization of CF and OAF N-glycans within the TNBC microenvironment was neither uniform across all N-glycan structures, nor was it strictly governed by the presence or absence of core fucosylation or OAF. This variation in distribution suggests that localization of fucosylation within the tumor microenvironment is influenced in a cellular N-glycan–specific manner rather than in relation to a general regulation of specific fucosylation linkages.
The observation of complementary (not overlapping) patterns of OAF versus CF N-glycosylation within the tumor microenvironment suggests that cell phenotypes may play a role in distribution patterns, likely through metabolic mechanisms affected by tumor gradients. Indeed, core fucosylation, solely catalyzed by fucosyltransferase (FUT) 8, is a critical regulator of receptor function and signal transduction. Elevated FUT8 expression has been positively correlated with epithelial–mesenchymal transition and increased tumor invasiveness and proliferation across multiple cancers, including breast, lung, and prostate cancers (
30
). In TNBC specifically, FUT8 knockdown rescues immunosuppressive glycan features, suggesting that FUT8 contributes to immune evasion mechanisms (
27
). Alternatively, OAF is catalyzed by a subset of FUTs, primarily including FUT3, FUT4, FUT5, FUT6, FUT7, and FUT9 to FUT11, which regulate the addition of terminal fucose residues in α1,3/4 linkages. Several of these enzymes show variable expression across breast cancer. One study showed that increased levels of FUT4, 5, 6, 10, and 11 in breast cancer cells correlated with increased migration, proliferation, and expression of angiogenesis-related genes, including
VEGFA
,
VEGFR1
,
VEGFR2
, and
FGF2
(
31
). Enzymes such as FUT3 and FUT6 facilitate the presentation of sialyl Lewis X and sialyl Lewis A antigens, which are essential for selectin-mediated adhesion to vascular endothelium. These modifications facilitate circulating tumor cell survival and vascular adhesion during metastasis (
32
). Furthermore, in TNBC, FUT7 expression has been linked to regulatory T-cell and macrophage cell infiltration and exhausted T-cell markers, and its overexpression has been linked to poor prognosis in TNBC (
33
). These enzyme-specific roles provide further context for the effects of CF and OAF N-glycans.
Spatial localization showed that OAF intensity was generally higher within the tumor regions, albeit in a heterogeneous manner, reinforcing its role in shaping the tumor microenvironment. The observed upregulation of OAF N-glycans across different stages of TNBC supports an involvement in tumor progression. Stage I tumors exhibited low OAF expression, consistent with prior reports indicating that early-stage tumors rely on less complex glycan structures (
34
,
35
). In TNBC tumors at higher stages, particularly stage III, a pronounced upregulation in the expression of OAF glycans was observed, implicating that these glycans contribute to a more aggressive tumor phenotype. Previous studies have shown that OAF N-glycans influence TNBC cellular mechanisms to increase epithelial–mesenchymal transitions and migration (
18
), which are critical in the spread and growth of cancer. Interestingly, a reduction in OAF N-glycan expression was noted in stage IV TNBC, which may reflect a metabolic adaptation favoring energy adaptation in which the tumor cells downregulate certain glycosylation pathways, such as fucosylation, to optimize energy utilization and support metastatic colonization (
36
–
39
). TNBC tumors have been shown to have higher glutamine consumption than other breast cancers, resulting in glutamine depletion in advanced tumors (
40
,
41
). A potential is that this metabolic change could signal the reprogramming needed to adapt to the depleted microenvironment and drive metastasis (
42
,
43
). In this scenario, the composition of the local microenvironment dictates the metabolic pathways used by the tumor cells that dissociate for metastasis. TNBC cell line studies have shown that TNBC is characterized by a glycolytic phenotype, with increased glucose uptake and lactate secretion (
36
). However, under metabolic stress or during metastasis, TNBC cells shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation or fatty acid oxidation to meet energy demands (
44
). This metabolic shift can influence the expression of glycosyltransferases and, consequently, the glycosylation patterns on cell-surface proteins (
38
). The significant changes in the tumor microenvironment across stages support that OAF glycans play an integral role in the transition from localized tumor growth to more advanced, metastatic disease.
A key objective of this investigation was the identification of glycan biomarkers predictive of clinical outcomes. This revealed a total of 68 glycans that were associated with survival. Of the N-glycans associated with outcomes, 8 were classified as CF, 36 as OAF, and 24 were non-fucosylated, underscoring the predominant role of OAF in outcome prediction. This is supported by recent work using lectin staining reporting that patients with TNBC and high expression of OAF N-glycans containing sialyl Lewis A and sialyl Lewis X motifs showed a 3 year decrease in free survival compared with low expression patterns (
45
). Here, OAF N-glycans contributed to mechanisms supporting TNBC proliferation and invasion capacity. Concordantly, our data show that high OAF expression correlates with poor prognosis, and these glycan signatures are detectable in early-stage diseases. In fact, 21 OAF N-glycans in our TNBC cohort were found to be significantly associated with both tumor stage and patient survival (Supplementary Table S6), thus highlighting their potential utility as early diagnostic or prognostic markers.
Notably, polylactosamine-containing OAF N-glycans were among the most strongly associated with reduced patient survival. This association was evident from the initial GlcNAc extensions on tetra-antennary structures to fully extended forms. Polylactosamine N-glycans have previously been identified as significant biomarkers in HER2+ breast cancer and TNBC, with growing evidence linking expression to poor patient outcomes and decreased survival rates (
17
,
46
). The aforementioned studies contradict the current work, as they report significant associations of CF polylactosamines by lectin motif staining in mouse models and in a small cohort of resected TNBC tumors. The current study uses a focused cohort of the same ancestry to systematically demonstrate that OAF polylactosamines associate with survival and increase by stage compared with their CF counterparts. However, previous studies have shown that increased expression of polylactosamine N-glycans in tumor cells is associated with increased tumor aggressiveness, enhanced metastasis, and a higher likelihood of resistance to standard treatments (
47
). In models of metastatic melanoma, polylactosamine expression increases cell adhesion as a high affinity ligand to galectin-3 that is expressed on specific organ endothelium such as the lung (
48
). According to the “seed and soil” theory of metastasis (
49
,
50
), TNBC tumor cell polylactosamine expression represents a positive adaptation to organ types enriched with galectin-3. Indeed, although nearly all organ tissues express galectin-3, the highest levels are found in the lung, brain, kidney, and bone (
51
), which are common TNBC metastatic sites (
52
). Additionally, the altered polylactosamine patterns may contribute to the promotion of tumor evasion and inflammatory responses, further complicating treatment strategies (
53
). The detection of OAF polylactosamines in early stages of TNBC tumors and links to survival outcomes define a high potential for use as a prognostic marker of more aggressive tumors.
Although this is the first report of the spatial landscape of fucosylated N-glycans in TNBC, there are limitations to the study. Although our findings are descriptive, the signatures are derived from clinically archived and clinically annotated tissue and at minimum suggest potential roles for N-glycosylation in tumor microenvironment interactions that control progression and overall survival. It is important to note that some of the N-glycosylation features identified in this study could reflect underlying ancestry-related glycomic variations in addition to tumor microenvironment–associated changes. Although our cohort, composed exclusively of African American women, offers a critical and underrepresented perspective in TNBC research, the lack of matched glycomic datasets from other ancestries limits our ability to definitively separate ancestry-specific signatures from tumor progression–associated features. Because of this, we cannot conclude whether the glycomic alterations identified in this study are broadly generalizable or enriched in African American patients. Comparative analyses across diverse populations will be essential to disentangle ancestry-driven variation from tumor-intrinsic biology and evaluate the potential of the identified glycomic markers as broadly applicable or ancestry-specific biomarkers. Finally, we do not know what cell types carry these signatures, nor do we know which proteins on specific cell types express the N-glycans found associated with staging and survival. Such data could point to distinct cell signaling mechanisms or relate these N-glycan modifications to mechanisms of the tissue microenvironment, where cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions play a role in TNBC progression. Such data could point to distinct cell signaling mechanisms or relate these N-glycan modifications to mechanisms of the tissue microenvironment, where the collective cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions play a role in TNBC progression.
There are many future directions to take that bridge the current findings on N-glycan fucosylation within the TNBC microenvironment with mechanistic insights. Investigations should systematically examine FUT or fucosidase by gain/loss of function in processes of tumor cell proliferation and survival. Such studies would systematically examine if altering the pool of OAF N-glycans in TNBC tumor cell lines by silencing or deleting critical glycogenes can regulate tumor cell survival or aggressiveness of the tumor cells, ideally measuring metabolic flux along with shifts in N-glycosylation. Glycogene silencing or deletion related to polylactosamine branching (B3GNT2 and B4GALT), in which polylactosamines were found increased in this study, could be used to further define mechanisms of polylactosamines involved in tumor survival, proliferation, and metastasis, potentially leading to treatments that block polylactosamine synthesis in patients with high-risk TNBC. As the current study detected that it is specific OAF glycans and not all OAF N-glycans involved in survival, it would be critical to identify which proteins within the tumor cells are carrying the specific OAF N-glycans, pointing toward the need for single–cell type glycopeptide analysis. Past work has shown that pools of N-glycans to individual N-glycan on target proteins can contribute to therapeutic resistance, proliferative, or metastatic events within tumor cells (
54
–
58
). However, changes to fucosylated N-glycans on immune cells may also alter immune homing and convert from pro-inflammatory to supporting tumor growth (
30
,
59
–
63
). This emphasizes the importance of studies modeling the tumor microenvironment in a way that evaluates altering glycosylation of either immune cell types or tumor cells, further highlighting the potential for mechanisms of the tumor microenvironment involving cell–cell or cell–extracellular cross-talk. An additional concept for investigation is that metabolic reprogramming involving glutamine stores may contribute to changes in OAF. In the current study, high levels of specific OAF associated with poor survival and increased with staging, utilizing glutamine for the production of branched and polylactosamine N-glycans. Glutamine consumption is known to be increased in TNBC subtypes, and elegant studies have shown that TNBC cell lines leverage glutaminolysis to replenish tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates (
64
). Glutamine metabolism is altered by obesity, a risk factor for TNBC (
65
,
66
), and obesity causes imbalances in glutamine uptake that contribute to altered immune activation within the tumor microenvironment (
67
). Future studies that systematically screen TNBC cell lines altered by high-fat diets with stable isotopic labeling of glutamine (
68
) could provide insights into mechanisms of glutamine utilization with appropriate risk factors. As high-fat diet also changes immune cell activity, it would be critical to model the tumor microenvironment under high-fat diet conditions to capture how metabolic alterations influence immune cell flux around the tumor site. Additionally, inhibition of fucosylation at key points in metabolism and N-glycan synthesis could be evaluated particularly taking into account risk conditions in TNBC cell lines. Overall limitations to cell line studies are that they do not take into account the complex framework of cell–cell and cell–matrix sensory and resource consumption within the tumor microenvironment. Thus, significant mechanistic insights will be gained by multiomics studies that combine spatial single-cell transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, and spatial metabolomics to understand the spatial distribution of fucose patterns of poor survival. Clearly, this study points to multiple new avenues of research in understanding the mechanisms of the TNBC microenvironment.
This study underscores the critical role of N-glycosylation, particularly OAF, in shaping the tumor microenvironment and driving the progression of TNBC. Through spatial glycomics and survival association analyses, we demonstrate that it is more so specific OAF N-glycans, rather than CF N-glycans, that are linked to tumor stage, aggressiveness, and patient outcomes. The distinct spatial distribution of OAF and CF N-glycans suggests that their localization may be governed by N-glycan–specific, cell-intrinsic factors, potentially influenced by metabolic states within the tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, the intricate structure–dependent distribution of CF and OAF N-glycan isomers in the TNBC microenvironment suggests that localization is not solely determined by the type of fucosylation but by the specific structural configurations of the N-glycans. This structural specificity reflects the cellular metabolic adaptations that contribute to tumor heterogeneity and progression.
Importantly, the upregulation of OAF N-glycans across TNBC stages highlights their involvement in promoting aggressive tumor phenotypes. Among these, polylactosamine-containing OAF N-glycans emerged as robust markers of poor prognosis, detectable even at early disease stages. The survival-associated N-glycans—predominantly OAF-modified—underscore that distinct N-glycans have clinical relevance in early detection, prognostic assessment, and potential patient stratification in TNBC. Further investigation of these N-glycans by cellular phenotype and protein carriers may unlock new therapeutic targets and improve patient management. Current research continues work to understand the functional implications of these glycans, particularly their roles in immune evasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. An ultimate goal is to provide personalized treatment approaches that address the dynamic and complex nature of the TNBC tumor microenvironment.
